extra.message: User-controlled 'host' query parameter is concatenated directly into a shell command passed to os.system(). An attacker can inject arbitrary OS commands (e.g., '127.0.0.1; rm -rf /').

User-controlled 'fragment' query parameter is concatenated directly into a Jinja2 template string 'Result: ' + fragment and rendered. This allows Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI), enabling remote code execution via Jinja2 template syntax like '{{ config.__class__.__init__.__globals__["os"].popen("id").read() }}'.

User-controlled 'name' query parameter is used directly in file path construction via BASE_EXPORT_DIR / name and then written to. An attacker can use '../' traversal to write files to arbitrary locations outside the intended directory, potentially overwriting sensitive files like server configuration or application code.

User-controlled 'packet_ref' query parameter is used directly in file path construction via incoming_dir / packet_ref and then written to with request body bytes. An attacker can use '../' traversal to write arbitrary content to any path on the filesystem.

XMLParser is configured with load_dtd=True, resolve_entities=True, and no_network=False. This enables external entity resolution, allowing XXE attacks. An attacker can submit XML that reads local files (e.g., /etc/passwd) or performs SSRF via external DTDs.

The reset_password endpoint accepts a 'token' parameter but NEVER verifies it before updating the password. On line 1239, user.hashed_password is directly set to the new password hash with only an email lookup on line 1235. Anyone who knows a user's email can reset their password without any token validation, enabling account takeover.

cwe: CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function

extra.message: User-controlled 'card' query parameter is passed through Jinja2's |safe filter and rendered as HTML without escaping. Since 'card' is user-controlled, an attacker can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript by passing a payload like '<script>alert(document.cookie)</script>' as the 'card' parameter.
User-controlled 'lane' query parameter is passed directly to RedirectResponse() without validation. An attacker can redirect users to arbitrary external URLs, enabling phishing attacks.

SSL certificate verification is explicitly disabled using ssl._create_unverified_context() for an HTTPS request. This makes the connection vulnerable to Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attacks, allowing an attacker to intercept or modify the response.

The Authorization header (Bearer token) is logged in plain text via logger.warning(). This exposes authentication tokens in log files, which could lead to account compromise if logs are accessed by unauthorized parties.

cwe: CWE-532: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File

extra.message: Ticket reply content is returned via the API without any HTML sanitization or encoding. An attacker can store malicious JavaScript in reply content (via POST /api/tickets/{id}/replies) which will be served to any user viewing the ticket. The same issue exists for KB article content (line 727) and internal notes (line 381).

The JWT signing SECRET_KEY falls back to a hardcoded, weak default value 'change-me-in-production-local-dev-only' when the SECRET_KEY environment variable is not set. If an attacker discovers this key, they can forge arbitrary JWT tokens and impersonate any user including admins.

The access_token cookie is set with httponly=True and samesite='lax' but without the secure=True flag. This means the authentication cookie can be transmitted over unencrypted HTTP connections, making it vulnerable to network sniffing and session hijacking.

cwe: CWE-614: Sensitive Cookie in HTTPS Session Without 'Secure' Attribute

extra.message: Content-Security-Policy is explicitly set to an empty string and X-XSS-Protection is set to '0' (line 85). This disables browser XSS protections and CSP, making the application more vulnerable to XSS and clickjacking attacks.

The demo password 'demo123' is hardcoded as a module-level constant and used as the password for all seed users including the admin account. If this seed data is used in a non-isolated environment, all accounts share a weak, publicly-known password.
